 19. Mr AM Mahbub Uddin also submits that initially the Shahid Asad Collegiate Girls' High School and College was selected for nationalization and an order was passed by the authority injuncting the appointment and promotion of the teachers and staff of the college and transfer of moveable and immoveable properties and this being the scenario, the process of nationalization proceeded to some extent; but all of a sudden, the petitioner was taken by surprise by issuance of the impugned Memo dated 4-1-2018 and considered from the above standpoint, the petitioner has a legitimate expectation in the matter of nationalization of Shahid Asad Collegiate Girls' High School and College. In support of his invocation of the principle of legitimate expectation, Mr AM Mahbub Uddin relies upon the decisions in the cases of the Chief Engineer, the Local Government and Engineering Department, LGED Bhaban, Agargaon, Sher-E-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka vs People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-Operatives, Bangladesh Secretariat, Ramna Dhaka, 32 BLD (AD) 177 = 17 BLC (AD) 91 and Joynanda Degree College, Kaharol, Dinajpur vs Ministry of Education, Bangladesh Secretariat, Ramna, Dhaka, 13 ALR 78. 

 21. Mr AKM Jaglul Haider Afric also submits that the selection of Shibpur Pilot Model High School in place of Shahid Asad Collegiate Girls' High School and College for nationalization is a policy decision of the Government and as this is a policy decision of the Government, it cannot be challenged under the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. In this regard, Mr AKM Jaglul Haider Afric draws our attention to an unreported decision dated 19-10-2017 of the High Court Division in the case of Nizam Uddin Azgor Ali Degree College, Sujanagar, Pabna vs Bangladesh and others rendered in Writ Petition No. 88 of 2017 which was eventually upheld by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal No. 4235 of 2017. 

 22. Mr AKM Jaglul Haider Afric next submits that বেসরকারি শিক্ষা প্রতিষ্ঠান জাতীয়করণ নীতিমালা, ২০১৬  (Guidelines of 2016) were not published in the official gazette and those Guidelines are Draft Guidelines having no force at all and this is why, the petitioner cannot rely upon the Guidelines of 2016 which were inadvertently referred to by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in the decision in the case of Joynanda Degree College, Kaharol, Dinajpur vs Ministry of Education, Bangladesh Secretariat, Ramna, Dhaka, 13 ALR 78 and this being the state of affairs, the invocation of the so-called Guidelines of 2016 is of no avail to the petitioner. 

 28. Generally speaking, a policy decision of the Government is not reviewable under Article 102 of the Constitution unless it is opposed thereto or to any provision of any law or unless it is ex-facie arbitrary or absurd or unreasonable. The job of nationalization of a Non-Government Secondary High School in the light of the criteria as contemplated by the Memo dated 15-9-2016 as evidenced by Annexure- '2' to the Supplementary Affidavit-in-Opposition dated 17-4-2019 is the job of the Executive. But the Executive must do its job in accordance with law. So the Memo dated 15-9-2016 must be kept in view while nationalizing a Non-Government Secondary High School by the Government. As the Guidelines of 2016 have not yet been published in the official gazette and as those Guidelines are Draft Guidelines, the petitioner cannot rely thereon in support of his case. 

 30. In the case of Food Corporation of India vs M/s Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries, AIR 1993 SC 1601, the Supreme Court of India held in paragraph 7: 

 "7. There is no unfettered discretion in public law: A public authority possesses powers only to use them for public good. This imposes the duty to act fairly and to adopt a procedure which is 'fair-play in action'. Due observance of this obligation as a part of good administration raises a reasonable or legitimate expectation in every citizen to be treated fairly in his interaction with the State and its instrumentalities, with this element forming a necessary component of the decision-making process in all State actions. To satisfy this requirement of non-arbitrariness in a State action, it is, therefore, necessary to consider and give due weight to the reasonable or legitimate expectations of the persons likely to be affected by the decision or else that unfairness in the exercise of the power may amount to an abuse or excess of power apart from affecting the bona fides of the decision in a given case. The decision so made would be exposed to challenge on the ground of arbitrariness. Rule of law does not completely eliminate discretion in the exercise of power, as it is unrealistic, but provides for control of its exercise by judicial review." 

 30. In the case of Mrs. Lalima Begum vs The Chairman, 1st Court of Settlement, Dhaka, 17 BLD 270 = 49 DLR 325, it was observed in paragraph 14: 

 32. In the case of Chingleput Bottlers vs Majestic Bottlers, reported in AIR 1984 SC 1030, the Indian Supreme Court has made certain observations which create an impression that the rule of natural justice is not applicable where it is a matter of privilege and no right or legitimate expectation is involved. But the application of the rule of natural justice is no longer tied to the dichotomy of right-privilege. It has been stated in "Administrative Law" by HWR Wade, 5th edition at page-465: "For the purpose of natural justice, the question which matters is not whether the claimant has some legal right, but whether the legal power is being exercised over him to his disadvantage. It is not a matter of property or of vested interests, but simply of the exercise of Governmental power in a manner which is fair •" In the American jurisdiction, the right-privilege dichotomy was used to deny due process hearing where no right was involved. But starting with Gonzalez vs Freeman (334 F. 2d 570), the Courts gradually shifted in favour of the privilege cases. In the words of Professor Schwartz, "The privilege-right dichotomy is in the process of being completely eroded" ("Administrative Law", 1976, Page-230). Article 31 of our Constitution incorporates the concept of procedural due process. So the English decisions expanding the frontiers of natural justice are fully applicable in Bangladesh. 

 33. The basic principle of fair procedure is that before taking any action against a person, the authority should give him notice of the case and afford him a fair opportunity to answer the case against him and to put his own case. The person sought to be affected must know the allegation and the materials to be used against him and he must be given a fair opportunity to correct or contradict them. The right to a fair hearing is now of universal application whenever a decision affecting the right or interest of a person is made. But such a notice is not required where the action does not affect the complaining party. 

 36. Thus there is malice in law where it is an act done wrongfully and wilfully without reasonable or probable cause and not necessarily an act done from ill-feeling and spite. It is a deliberate act in disregard of the rights of others. (State of AP vs Goverdhanlal Pitti, 4 SCC 739). If an authority acts on what are, justly and logically viewed, extraneous grounds or if an authority acts on a legally extraneous or obviously misconceived ground of action, it would be a case of malice in law. (Regional Manager vs Pawan Kumar Dubey, AIR 1976 SC 1766). 

 37. Malice in law is a malice which is implied by law in certain circumstances, even in the absence of malicious intention or improper motive. (Shearer vs Shield, [1914] AC 808). Colourable exercise of power is equated with malice in law and in such a case, it is not necessary to establish that the respondent was actuated by a bad motive. (Venkataraman vs India, AIR 1979 SC 49). 

 39. Ours is a written Constitution. It is axiomatic that judicial review is the soul of the Judiciary in a written Constitution. In recent times, judicial review of administrative action has become expansive and is becoming wider day by day. The traditional limitations have been vanishing and the sphere of judicial scrutiny is being expanded. Availability of reasons for any administrative action on the record assures credibility to the action; disciplines public conduct and improves the culture of accountability. Looking for reasons in support of such action provides an opportunity for an objective review in appropriate cases both by the administrative superior and by the judicial body.
